new_statements.quote: Im allgemeinen werden Stamm- und Afformativsilben mit gleichem Nachdruck gesprochen, so daß sich Haupt- oder Nebenakzent nicht unterscheiden läßt. Eine scheinbare Akzentuierung der Stammsilbe entsteht durch die weitgehende Reduktion der Auslautvokale [...]. Da auch die vor infigiertem li eintretenden Flüstervokale mit wesentlich geringerem als normalem Nachdruck gesprochen werden, so täuschen einzelne Wörter, wie z. B. kèléndi „Ohrgehänge“, leicht einen auf der vorletzten Silbe liegenden Starkton vor, während eine Verstärkung des Nachdrucks tatsächlich nicht stattfindet.
new_statements.translation: In general, stem and afformative syllables are spoken with equal force, so that no main or secondary accent can be distinguished. An apparent accentuation of the stem syllable arises from the extensive reduction of the final vowels [...]. Since the whispered vowels that appear before infixed li are also spoken with much less than normal force, individual words such as kèléndi 'ear-pendants' easily give the illusion of a strong stress on the penultimate syllable, whereas no reinforcement of force actually takes place.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kresh (as recorded by Struck) is a tone language (high/mid/low) with no word accent: all syllables carry equal force; the stem (first) syllable of a suffixed word, or the penult of words with a whispered pre-li vowel, merely sounds prominent because final/whispered vowels are reduced. Later sources on Kresh hear this as initial prominence: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Bongo-Bagirmi group incl. Kresh) 'stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel'; Santandrea 1976 says in Kresh disyllables 'both syllables are accented, though.. more evident in the first', with enclitics 'the accent lies on the first syllable and on the enclitic', and that some verb pairs 'differ both in tone and accent'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Struck: no main vs secondary accent distinguishable. Santandrea 1976 (snippet): with an enclitic/suffix, accent on the first syllable and on the enclitic, middle syllable unaccented.
new_statements.exceptions: Struck: apparent stem-syllable or penultimate prominence is a by-product of final-vowel reduction / whispered vowels before infixed li (e.g. kèléndi). Tucker & Bryan: occasionally stress on the second syllable when the first has a central vowel (group-level remark).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stem + afformative/suffix syllables), isolated words from Struck's own Kresh ('Gbaya, Dar Fertit') material; NOT the Dongo variety. The only description that treats Dongo itself (Santandrea 1976) is print-only; its snippets give no Dongo-specific stress statement. The Struck quote is reconstructed from overlapping scanned snippets (one elided clause about where final-vowel reduction is most frequent is given in full); the page image could not be verified by automated download.
new_statements.identity_note: No source seen says anything about stress in the Dongo variety itself. The quoted statement (Struck 1918) and the supporting snippets (Tucker & Bryan 1966; most of Santandrea 1976) describe Kresh / 'Gbaya (Dar Fertit)' generally, i.e. Glottolog gbay1288 'Kresh-Woro' [krs] and its Kreshic sisters, of which Dongo Kresh (dong1296) is one; Glottolog separates Dongo on the strength of Santandrea 1976: 10-11 ('Dongo, or Dango, stands obviously as a [language apart]' per Santandrea 1970 snippet). Santandrea 1976 is the only work whose phonology tables carry a Dongo column.

new_statements.quote: 2b. Stress Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI kala, snake, for instance. [sec. 3 Word Shape:] In KRESH, since the final vowels of words are always elided before the initial vowels of following words, the amount of vowel elision in the average sentence is very great

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for dong1296; the only existing statement is Struck 1918 (no distinguishable main/secondary accent in Kresh/'Gbaya'; the apparent stem-syllable accent is an artefact of far-reaching final-vowel reduction). Tucker & Bryan assert a normal initial stress for the whole group, i.e. a different type (stress present, initial) — hence 'contradicts'. The two agree on the surface fact (the first/stem syllable is the prominent one, most clearly when the final vowel is reduced/semi-mute); they disagree on whether to call it stress. Neither statement is Dongo-specific: T&B's is a group generalization not naming Kresh in the stress paragraph, and Struck's variety is the southern…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement over the Bongo-Bagirmi languages (whose 'Central languages' are the KRESH Group incl. Yulu-Binga, and Kara): stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and always on the first syllable when the second syllable has a semi-mute (reduced) vowel; occasionally on the second syllable when the first syllable contains a central vowel. Nothing said specifically about Kresh or Dongo stress; Kresh is named only among the languages analysed for (three-level) tone and for its wholesale elision of word-final vowels before a following initial vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress heard on the second syllable when the first syllable contains a central vowel; Stevenson's BAGIRMI kala 'snake' cited as an example of second-syllable stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat DONGO as a variety within the Kresh Group of their Bongo-Bagirmi chapter (it appears in the noun-gender, possessive-suffix and imperative tables: 'DONGO shows Animate/Inanimate distinction only', 'DONGO alone shows Exclusive/Inclusive'), but the stress paragraph (p. 64) is a statement over the whole Bongo-Bagirmi group and names only BAGIRMI as an example; KRESH is named in the tone paragraph and in the word-shape remark on final-vowel elision. The existing Struck 1918 statement describes the southern Kresh/Gbaya of the Biri-valley enclave (Kresh-Woro/gbay1288 area), not the northern Dongo variety, per the verified page-image identity note already in this folder.

readall_conflicts: Struck 1918 (existing statement; southern Kresh/'Gbaya' of the Biri-valley enclave, recorded from one speaker in Berlin) says stem and affix syllables are spoken with equal emphasis so that no main or secondary accent can be distinguished, the apparent stem-syllable accent arising only from the reduction of final vowels, and in fn. 9 p. 54 speaks of 'dem Fehlen des Starktons'. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (group-level, Bongo-Bagirmi languages including the Kresh Group) say stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel, with occasional second-syllable stress when the first syllable has a central vowel. The disagreement is about whether the first-syllable prominence counts as word stress (T&B: yes, initial; Struck: no, an artefact of final-vowel reduction), not about which syllable is prominent; both tie the prominence to reduced final vowels, and T&B independently note that Kresh always elides word-final vowels before a following initial vowel. No source opened makes a Dongo-specific stress statement.
